title: Why people join coworking spaces

source.rightsNotes: Original passage written for Studyworks Reading Coach; fictional study.

questionStemHtml: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text as a whole?
passageHtml: Sociologist Maya Trent's survey of 42 coworking spaces concluded that members join primarily to escape household distraction. Yet when Trent's team logged how members actually spent their hours, fewer than a third involved focused solo work; the balance went to conversations, introductions, and impromptu collaborations. Trent now argues that the survey answers reflect what members find easiest to justify — paying for productivity — while the logs capture a motive members rarely name: the wish to belong to a working community.

taskRubric.canonicalTask: Explain what role the second sentence plays in the structure of the passage.
requiredIdeas: describe the sentence's function relative to the rest of the passage, not its content alone
acceptableVariants: say why the author includes the second sentence
explain what the second sentence does for the argument
commonWrongTasks: decide whether coworking spaces are worthwhile

processingUnits.textHtml: Sociologist Maya Trent's survey of 42 coworking spaces concluded that members join primarily to escape household distraction.
requiredIdeas: a survey found members join coworking spaces to escape distraction at home
prohibitedDistortions: the survey was about employers rather than members

processingUnits.textHtml: Yet when Trent's team logged how members actually spent their hours, fewer than a third involved focused solo work; the balance went to conversations, introductions, and impromptu collaborations.
requiredIdeas: activity logs showed most time went to social interaction and collaboration
focused solo work was a minority of members' time
requiredRelations: contrast between what members said in the survey and what the logs showed they did
prohibitedDistortions: members did no focused work at all
the logs came from a different research team

processingUnits.textHtml: Trent now argues that the survey answers reflect what members find easiest to justify — paying for productivity — while the logs capture a motive members rarely name: the wish to belong to a working community.
requiredIdeas: Trent reinterprets the survey answers as easy-to-justify explanations
the logs are taken to reveal an unnamed motive: belonging to a community
requiredRelations: the log evidence leads Trent to reinterpret the survey responses
prohibitedDistortions: members deliberately lied on the survey
Trent discarded the survey as worthless

passageRubric.canonicalSummary: A survey suggested people join coworking spaces for distraction-free productivity, but activity logs showed most member time going to conversation and collaboration, leading the researcher to conclude that the survey captured a convenient justification while the real, rarely named motive is belonging to a working community.
requiredIdeas: survey: members say they join to escape distraction and be productive
logs: most observed time was social and collaborative rather than solo work
conclusion: the stated motive is a justification, the underlying motive is community
requiredRelations: contrast between reported motives and observed behavior
the observed behavior drives the reinterpretation of the survey answers
prohibitedDistortions: coworking spaces fail at supporting productivity
the survey and logs came from rival research teams

preanswerRubric.canonicalPreanswer: The second sentence supplies observed-behavior evidence that conflicts with the survey finding, setting up the reinterpretation in the final sentence.
requiredIdeas: it introduces evidence about what members actually did
that evidence complicates or undercuts the survey finding from the first sentence
acceptableVariants: it presents data that contradicts sentence one and sets up the conclusion
it provides the twist the final reinterpretation builds on
prohibitedClaims: it introduces an unrelated new research question

choices.label: A
choices.html: It restates the claim introduced in the first sentence in more precise statistical terms.
choices.rationaleHtml: The second sentence does not restate the survey finding — it reports behavior that conflicts with it, signaled by 'Yet.'

choices.label: B
choices.html: It presents a competing conclusion drawn by a rival research group.
choices.rationaleHtml: The logging was done by Trent's own team, not a rival group.

choices.label: C
choices.html: It introduces observational evidence that complicates the survey finding reported in the first sentence.
choices.rationaleHtml: Correct. The sentence contrasts what members actually did with what the survey said they wanted, which is exactly what the final sentence resolves.

choices.label: D
choices.html: It concedes a limitation of the logging method before defending its reliability.
choices.rationaleHtml: The passage never questions or defends the logging method; this adds a move the text does not make.
